summary: Bilateral BGP sessions between exchange participants have long been the norm, but the overhead of managing many of them has made route servers popular. This informational document describes operational considerations for running and using route servers at Internet Exchange Points. It complements the route server specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If one post office passes mail between many neighbors, someone must run it well. This is advice for people who run or use that post office at an internet exchange point.

subtitle: Operational guidance for running and using BGP route servers at Internet Exchange Points.

tldr.problem: Internet Exchange Points connect hundreds of networks through BGP routing. Traditionally, each network sets up direct BGP sessions with every other network on the exchange (bilateral peering), requiring administrative overhead that scales quadratically with the number of participants.
tldr.mechanism: Route servers (specialized BGP speakers) redistribute routes received from all clients to all other clients according to policy. Each participant needs only one BGP session to the route server instead of sessions with every other participant, reducing sessions from n*(n-1)/2 to n.
tldr.outcome: Route servers dramatically simplify IXP operations and enable new participants to gain immediate interconnection with all others, but operators must address operational challenges including path hiding, scaling limits, security vulnerabilities, and layer 2 problems.

today: RFC 7948 is an Informational RFC published in September 2016 that represents IETF community consensus on operational best practices. It remains the primary operational reference for Internet Exchange Points deploying or operating BGP route servers.

sections.title: BGP Peering at Internet Exchanges
sections.content:
An Internet Exchange Point (IXP) is a facility where many networks connect to exchange traffic and routing information. Historically, networks at an IXP established bilateral BGP sessions: each network pair configures a BGP session between their routers to exchange reachability information about the networks they control. For an exchange with n participants that all want to connect to all others, this requires n*(n-1)/2 sessions—a full mesh of connections.

The administrative overhead scales quadratically. When a new network joins, existing participants must all configure a BGP session with the newcomer. For a large IXP with hundreds of members, each new participant triggers dozens of configuration changes across the exchange. Route servers eliminate this problem by acting as a multilateral interconnection hub. Instead of configuring BGP with every other network, each participant configures a single session to the route server, receiving routes from all others in return. This reduces sessions from n*(n-1)/2 to n and allows new participants to immediately interconnect with all others without configuration changes to existing members.
sections.plainLanguage: Bilateral is like everyone calling everyone else. If you have 100 people and want full mesh, you need 5,000 calls. A route server is like a conference call where 100 people call one switchboard number and hear everyone.

sections.title: How Route Servers Work
sections.content:
A route server is not a router: it receives BGP routes from clients, stores them in a Loc-RIB (Local Routing Information Base) for each client, applies configured routing policies, and sends updated routes to clients. Critically, the route server preserves the NEXT_HOP attribute unchanged. This attribute specifies the IP address to use to reach the announced destination; leaving it pointing to the announcing client allows direct traffic flow between clients without the route server touching data.

Route server operators must carefully manage several operational challenges. Path hiding occurs when the route server applies conflicting policies to different clients viewing the same destination, causing some clients to receive incomplete routing information. Scaling is a super-linear problem: the route server's computational requirements scale approximately as O(P * N), where P is the number of unique paths and N is the number of clients with unique policies. Network bandwidth requirements scale even worse at O(N^2) in the worst case. Prefix leakage happens when a misconfigured client announces routes it should not, potentially spreading to all other clients and beyond. Route server operators must implement inbound prefix filtering and per-client limits to prevent damage.
sections.plainLanguage: A route server listens to everyone, remembers who said what, and tells everyone else. But it has to be careful about what it tells each person, it can get overwhelmed if there are too many people, and if one person says the wrong thing, it might spread to everyone.

sections.title: Operational and Security Challenges
sections.content:
Scaling issues require careful attention. For large IXPs, operators can deploy multiple route servers and selectively split prefixes across them (destination splitting) to reduce each server's load. They can also merge clients with identical routing policies into a single view or use view decomposition to track delta differences from a master view, reducing memory requirements.

Layer 2 reachability problems specific to route servers can cause serious outages. If two IXP participants can reach the route server but cannot reach each other due to a switch forwarding bug, traffic between them will fail, but only for traffic destined to each other—a silent failure mode that bilateral peering would not produce. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) can partially mitigate this, but currently offers no automatic session configuration between route server clients.

BGP NEXT_HOP hijacking is a critical security risk. A route server client can announce BGP routes with NEXT_HOP set to a different IXP participant's address, redirecting traffic through that participant or causing denial-of-service. Route server operators SHOULD validate that announced NEXT_HOP values match the announcing client's interface address, and SHOULD drop routes where NEXT_HOP points to a different AS, with exceptions only for traffic engineering within the same AS. Route servers should also disable AS_PATH consistency checks on clients (since the route server does not prepend AS numbers) and use robust BGP configuration following RFC 7454 BGP operations best practices.
sections.plainLanguage: Too many routes crash the server. Broken network switches can cause strange failures. Bad clients can trick the server into redirecting someone else's traffic, like address spoofing a package. Operators need to prevent these.

sections.title: Routing Policy and Redundancy
sections.content:
Route servers support multiple mechanisms for clients to express routing policies. BGP Communities allow clients to tag routes with community values that the route server uses to decide which clients receive which routes. However, standard and extended communities are limited to 6 octets total, forcing route server operators to plan carefully for compatibility with 4-octet AS numbers. Alternatively, operators can use Internet Routing Registries (IRRDBs) to look up client policies in standards-based databases, or build their own client-accessible policy database allowing clients to specify routing policies without modifying the route server configuration.

Redundancy is essential for reliability. The RFC recommends deploying multiple route servers on each Layer 2 domain at an IXP, with identical configuration so that all clients receive identical route information from each server. If one route server fails, clients continue receiving routes from others. Operators need not use identical BGP implementations or operating systems across servers, but must ensure routing views remain synchronized.
sections.plainLanguage: Route servers can use labels on routes to decide who gets what. Or they can look up policies in a shared database. They need backups in case one fails, so traffic keeps flowing.

sections.title: Best Practices for Route Server Operations
sections.content:
Successful route server deployment requires implementing multiple protective measures. Inbound prefix filtering prevents leakage of unauthorized routes, either through explicit per-client prefix limits (simpler but less precise) or detailed filter lists (more reliable but resource-intensive). Operators deploying detailed filters should build automated systems to compare announced prefixes against configured filter lists, alerting operators to discrepancies between published policies and actual behavior.

Route servers should implement automatic monitoring to detect when policies and actual routing information diverge. Many network operators do not carefully maintain published policies, creating security risks. Comparing the Adj-RIB-In (what the route server receives from each client) against configured prefix lists can surface policy violations early. Additionally, route servers should operate in compliance with RFC 7454's BGP security recommendations for hardening, logging, and monitoring, adjusted as needed for the route server context. The combination of technical controls (prefix filtering, NEXT_HOP validation), redundancy (multiple servers), monitoring (policy compliance checks), and standards compliance (RFC 7454) provides a robust operational foundation for reliable IXP interconnection.
sections.plainLanguage: Good operations mean checking what clients announce against what they said they would announce, having backup servers, following security best practices, and watching for trouble.
